thread.title: PA budget gives 60,000 state retirees first pension boost since 2001 - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: PA budget gives 60,000 state retirees first pension boost since 2001 - NewsBreak

author: Matthew Rink
title: PA budget gives 60,000 state retirees first pension boost since 2001 - NewsBreak
text:
By Matthew Rink ,
19 hours ago It's been more than two decades since some of the longest retired teachers and other public servants, including some firefighters and police officers, have received an increase in their pension, even as inflation has cut their buying power in half.
However, the newly minted 2026-2027 Pennsylvania budget remedies what many say was long-overdue. Some 60,000 retirees of the Public School Employees' Retirement System and the State Employees' Retirement System, as well as some firefighters and police officers, all of whom retired prior to July 2, 2001, will receive increases of 15% to 24.5%, which on average amounts to $250 more per month for PSERS retirees and $195 more per month for SERS retirees.
The provision was made as part of the $50.8 billion spending plan signed into law Sunday by Gov. Josh Shapiro.
Budget passes: How did Pennsylvania up its rainy day fund in this year's budget?
Exempt from 2001 reforms Most of these workers, who are now in their 80s and 90s, have been receiving pension benefits of less than $20,000 annually.
PSERS and SERS oversee the pensions of some 750,000 current and former state employees, but the increases will only affect those 60,000 people who retired before the Pennsylvania legislature enacted Act 9 of 2001. Act 9 was a major pension system overhaul that increased employee contributions from 6.25% to 7.5% in order to fund enhanced benefits for retirees.
However, the pre-Act 9 retirees were exempt from the provision. The last time they saw a cost-of-living increase in their pension was 2001.
'Finally made good on our promise' “These are the men and women who shaped our state’s and our children’s futures, and for more than 20 years, they were left trying to get by on pensions that didn’t keep up,” said Rep. Steve Malagari, a Montgomery County Democrat who has been sponsoring separate legislation since the 2023-2024 session to fix the issue. “The last COLA these retirees saw was in 2001. Since then, the cost of medicine, groceries and housing has only gone up. Today, we’ve finally made good on our promise to these public servants in their final years.”
“We are encouraged that the budget provides funding for a Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) for retired public employees," Angela Ferritto, president of the Pennsylvania AFL-CIO, said in a statement. "These long-overdue increases recognize the contributions of retired workers who have seen their pensions lose purchasing power after years of inflation.”
While Malagari, the Democrat, reintroduced his legislation in the House in 2025 as H.B. 411 , Republican state Sen. Frank Ferry introduced similar legislation in the Senate last year, S.B. 721 .
The increases cost $88.8 million annually for PSERS and $38.4 million for SERS, but were funded through existing grant programs, so they will have no impact on the general fund, school districts or local governments.
Matthew Rink is a USA TODAY Network Pennsylvania investigative journalist.
This article originally appeared on Erie Times-News: PA budget gives 60,000 state retirees first pension boost since 2001
